'''Sarah Kirsch''' ({{IPA|de|ˈzaː.ʁa ˈkɪʁʃ|lang|De-Sarah Kirsch.ogg}}; 16 April 1935 – 5 May 2013) was a German poet.<ref name=dw>{{cite web |url=http://www.dw.de/widely-regarded-german-lyricist-sarah-kirsch-dies/a-16830401 |title=Widely regarded German lyricist Sarah Kirsch dies |publisher=[[Deutsche Welle|DW]] |date=22 May 2013 |access-date=27 May 2013}}</ref>

==Biography==
Sarah Kirsch was originally born '''Ingrid Bernstein''' in [[Hohenstein, Thuringia|Limlingerode]], [[Prussian Saxony]] but had changed her first name to Sarah in order to protest against [[antisemitism]].<ref name=dw/> She studied biology in [[University of Halle-Wittenberg|Halle]] and literature at the [[German Institute for Literature|Johannes R. Becher Institute for Literature]] in [[University of Leipzig|Leipzig]].<ref name=dw/> In 1965, she co-wrote a book of poems with writer [[Rainer Kirsch]], to whom she was married for nine years, from 1960 to 1968.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Shaffer|first1=E.S.|title=Comparative Criticism: Volume 7, Boundaries of Literature|date=1986|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=9780521332019|page=183|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MhVClkBc1E8C&q=Rainer+Kirsch+sarah+1965&pg=PA183}}</ref> She protested against [[East Germany]]'s expulsion of [[Wolf Biermann]] in 1976, which led to her exclusion from the [[Socialist Unity Party of Germany]] (SED).<ref name=dw/> One year later she left the country herself, nevertheless being critical of the West as well. Sarah Kirsch won many prizes and honours including the German international literary [[Petrarca-Preis]] in 1976, the [[Peter Huchel Prize]] in 1993 and the [[Georg Büchner Prize]] in 1996.<ref name=dw/> She died in May 2013 following a brief illness.<ref name=dw/><ref name=Death>{{cite news |title=Dichterin Sarah Kirsch ist tot |url=http://www.spiegel.de/kultur/literatur/sarah-kirsch-ist-tot-a-901212.html |work=[[Der Spiegel]] |date=22 May 2013 |language=de |access-date=22 May 2013}}</ref>

==Work==
Sarah Kirsch is known both for her poetry and her (lyrically inflected) prose. She also translated children's books into German.<ref>{{Cite web| last = Witalec| first = Janet| title = Kirsch, Sarah - Introduction| publisher = Gale Cengage| url=http://www.enotes.com/contemporary-literary-criticism/kirsch-sarah| access-date = 12 April 2010 }}</ref> According to ''[[complete review]]''<!--lower cap-->, "the great German-language post-war poets were largely [[East German]] (or Austrian) born in the mid to late 1930s which included towering figures such as [[Volker Braun]], [[Heinz Czechowski]]" and Sarah Kirsch who was "the most prominent female representative of that generation."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.complete-review.com/saloon/archive/201305c.htm#hk1 |title=Sarah Kirsch (1935-2013)  |work=[[complete review]] |date=27 May 2013 |access-date=27 May 2013}}</ref> [[Andreas Dorschel]] credits her prose with "highly flexible spelling, nuanced in puns, archaisms, turns of dialect, peculiar rhythms, poetic imagery".<ref>Andreas Dorschel, 'Gläserne Leitern', ''Süddeutsche Zeitung'' Nr. 273, 24 November 2008, p. 14: "Prosa von höchst beweglicher Orthographie, nuanciert in Wortspielen, Archaismen, Wendungen des Dialekts, eigentümlichen Rhythmen, Bildern".</ref>
